The municipal clock stopped at 3:17, and for the first time in forty years, nobody called Martin.

He waited beside the telephone until four.

Then he put on his coat, took his tools, and walked into town.

The clock stood above the old library, which was now a place where people rented desks. Through its tall windows he could see young people wearing headphones, each seated before a small luminous rectangle. They looked like monks engaged in a religion that required excellent posture but seldom achieved it.

At reception, a woman asked whether he had booked a room.

“I’ve come about the clock.”

She looked at the clock on her computer.

“The other one,” he said.

“Oh. Right.”

She made a phone call. He examined a bowl of green apples so polished they appeared to be a statement about apples rather than something to eat.

A man arrived wearing shoes without socks.

“We were actually discussing this,” the man said. “Whether it’s necessary to maintain it.”

“It’s stopped.”

“Yes. Whether that’s a problem.”

Martin had brought several screwdrivers, a small oil bottle, and the key to the clock chamber. He had brought nothing suitable for this conversation.

“It tells the time.”

“Everyone has the time.”

Above them, beyond the refurbished ceiling and the air ducts, the mechanism waited. Martin knew its noises: the dry click before release, the weight descending in its shaft, the slight complaint of a bearing he had meant to replace last spring.

“I could take a look,” he said.

The man consulted his phone.

“As long as there’s no charge.”

***

Inside the tower, the air smelled of dust and old grease.

Martin stood still until his breathing settled. The stairs had become steeper over the years, despite remaining precisely the same stairs.

The fault was simple. A pin had worked loose and lodged where it ought not to be. He found it, freed it, and held it in his palm.

“That’s all you are,” he said.

From below came the muffled sound of a meeting.

He could repair the clock in twenty minutes. Ten, if his hands behaved. Then he could go home, wash the oil from his fingers, and eat the soup his daughter had left in the refrigerator, labeled TUESDAY, as if he might otherwise attempt to eat Thursday.

Instead, he sat on the wooden stool.

There were names carved beneath its seat. He knew because he had carved one himself at nineteen. His predecessor had caught him doing it.

“If you want your name on something,” old Bell had said, “make something.”

Then Bell had turned the stool over and shown him his own name.

Martin reached beneath the seat. His fingers found the letters without difficulty.

***

At five, footsteps sounded on the stairs.

The receptionist appeared carrying two mugs.

“I thought you might want tea.”

“Thank you.”

She handed him one and looked around.

“I’ve worked here eight months. I didn’t know all this was up here.”

“Where did you think the clock was?”

“On the outside.”

He smiled, and she did too.

She watched him retrieve the loose pin.

“Is it expensive?”

“No.”

“Can you fix it?”

“Yes.”

“Are you going to?”

He turned the pin between his fingers.

“They don’t seem to mind if I don’t.”

She set her mug on the windowsill and peered through a gap beside the clock face.

“My bus stop’s down there,” she said. “I look up when I’m waiting.”

“You have a phone.”

“It’s usually in my bag.”

He took a small pair of pliers from his case.

“Could you hold this?”

She came over and steadied the inspection lamp while he worked. Her sleeve brushed the great brass wheel.

“Careful there,” he said. “It’ll move.”

***

When the clock started, she jumped.

The sound filled the chamber: one click, another, then the familiar sequence, uneven for a moment before settling.

Martin watched the repaired joint through several cycles.

The woman looked pleased.

“Should I tell someone?”

“Tell the man downstairs it’ll need a proper service before winter.”

“Will you do it?”

“If he asks.”

She nodded as though this were a perfectly workable arrangement.

They finished their tea. Martin packed his tools, leaving the lamp until last.

At the foot of the stairs, she asked his name.

“Martin.”

“I’m Leah.”

She wrote both names on a note beside her keyboard: his with a telephone number, hers beneath *clock service—October*. Then she gave him a sheet of paper for an invoice.

“He said no charge,” Martin told her.

“He says that about everything. Put down what it costs.”

***

Outside, Martin stopped across the road and looked up.

The minute hand advanced.

Below it, a boy was trying to persuade a reluctant dog past the butcher’s. Someone dropped a bag of oranges. Two people bent to help and bumped their heads.

Martin checked his watch against the clock.

Then he went home to Tuesday’s soup, carrying his empty flask and an apple Leah had insisted was real.
